chapters.title: A Runaway Reef
chapters.summary: In 1866 ships around the world report an enormous, glowing, spindle-shaped thing at sea, faster and bigger than any whale. In 1867 it rams two liners, punching a clean triangular hole in the Cunard steamer Scotia, and the public demands that the seas be rid of the "monster."
details: The narrator looks back on 1866, the year seamen everywhere began reporting "an enormous thing" at sea: long, spindle-shaped, sometimes glowing, and far bigger and faster than any known whale. The steamer Governor Higginson sees it off Australia, where Captain Baker takes it for an uncharted reef until it shoots two waterspouts into the air. Within days other ships sight it hundreds of leagues away, and two ships in the Atlantic estimate its length at over 350 feet.

The "monster question" becomes a craze. Cafés sing about it, newspapers mock it, scientific journals argue over it, and old tales of krakens and sea serpents are dragged back into print. After six months of debate a satirical columnist laughs the creature out of existence, and by early 1867 the subject seems dead.

Then the thing turns dangerous. In March the Moravian strikes an uncharted "rock" at night and later finds part of its keel smashed. In April the Scotia, one of the famous Cunard line's finest steamers, is struck below the waterline during afternoon tea. Captain Anderson keeps her afloat thanks to her watertight compartments and limps into Liverpool. In dry dock the engineers find a perfect triangular hole in her iron hull, as if punched by a tool of uncommon toughness that then pulled itself back out.
After this, every unexplained shipwreck is blamed on the monster, and with ocean travel now seen as unsafe, the public demands that it be hunted down at any cost.

chapters.title: The Pros and Cons
chapters.summary: The narrator, Professor Pierre Aronnax of the Paris Museum, is in New York when the Scotia affair breaks, and publishes an article arguing that the culprit is a giant narwhal. The United States fits out the frigate Abraham Lincoln to hunt it, and Aronnax is invited aboard.
details: The narrator introduces himself: Pierre Aronnax, Assistant Professor at the Paris Museum of Natural History, just back from a six-month expedition to the Nebraska badlands and waiting in New York to sail home. By now the theories of a drifting reef or wreck have been dropped, leaving two camps: a colossal sea creature, or an "underwater boat" of tremendous power. The boat theory collapses when every government formally denies building such a weapon, and a private inventor seems unlikely to have built one in secret.

As the author of a well-known two-volume work, The Mysteries of the Great Ocean Depths, Aronnax is pressed for his opinion and writes an article for The New York Herald. He argues that either the unknown depths hide species science has never seen, or the creature is a known animal on a giant scale: a narwhal, or "sea unicorn," five or ten times normal size, whose ivory tusk could pierce a steamer's hull. He leaves himself a loophole (it might be "something else entirely") to protect his dignity, but privately he now believes in the monster.

The article is widely debated, and practical opinion in America and England turns to destroying the creature. In New York the fast frigate Abraham Lincoln is armed under Commander Farragut, but the monster vanishes for two months. On June 2 news comes that a steamer saw it in the northern Pacific. Three hours before the frigate sails, Aronnax receives a letter from J. B. Hobson, Secretary of the Navy, inviting him to join the expedition as France's representative.

chapters.title: As Master Wishes
chapters.summary: Aronnax instantly accepts the invitation and tells his unflappable servant Conseil to pack. They rush to Brooklyn, are welcomed aboard by Commander Farragut, and the Abraham Lincoln steams out of New York to cheering crowds.
details: Though exhausted and longing for Paris, Aronnax decides on the spot that hunting the monster is his true calling, and accepts. He calls for Conseil, his Flemish manservant of ten years: thirty years old, calm, hardworking, never surprised, a walking expert in biological classification who knows nothing of actual animals, and so formal that he addresses Aronnax only in the third person as "master." Aronnax, we learn, is forty.

Aronnax warns Conseil that this voyage could be long and dangerous, the kind people don't always come back from. Conseil answers each warning with "As master wishes" and packs the trunks in a quarter of an hour. Aronnax leaves orders to ship his fossil collections and his live babirusa (a wild pig) to Paris.

At the Brooklyn pier Commander Farragut welcomes Aronnax aboard the Abraham Lincoln, a high-speed frigate built for the hunt. Minutes later the ship casts off, escorted by about a hundred small boats while huge crowds cheer from the shores. By evening it is steaming into the open Atlantic.

chapters.title: Ned Land
chapters.summary: Aboard the Abraham Lincoln everyone believes in the monster except Ned Land, the Canadian "King of Harpooners." Off Patagonia, Aronnax tries to convince him with calculations about deep-sea pressure, but Ned stays skeptical.
details: Commander Farragut believes in the monster as an article of faith and has vowed to rid the seas of it. His officers and crew share his zeal, helped along by a $2,000 reward for whoever sights it first. The frigate carries every kind of whaling weapon, from hand harpoons to a modern breech-loading cannon. Of everyone aboard, only Conseil seems uninterested.

The ship's greatest weapon is Ned Land, a Canadian harpooner of about forty from an old Quebec fishing family: very tall, powerfully built, unsociable, headstrong and quick to anger, with a remarkably strong gaze. He takes a liking to Aronnax because they share French, and he tells him stories of his whaling adventures in the polar seas.

Yet Ned doesn't believe in the monster. On the evening of June 25, off the coast of Patagonia, Aronnax presses him. Ned says no whale he has ever hunted could pierce a steamer's iron plates. Aronnax explains water pressure, which crushes harder the deeper you go: any animal living in the depths would need a body as tough as an armored warship, and such a mass could strike a hull like an express train. Ned is staggered by the numbers but won't give in, and falls back on "it just couldn't be true!" Aronnax remains sure the creature is a vertebrate, a mammal and a cetacean, and that catching it depends first on finding it.

chapters.title: At Random!
chapters.summary: Ned Land shows his skill by harpooning two whales at once. The Abraham Lincoln rounds Cape Horn and searches the northern Pacific in vain for three months until the crew nearly mutinies. Farragut asks for three more days, and on the last night Ned shouts that the thing has been sighted.
details: Off the Falkland Islands, an American whaler asks for Ned's help, and he harpoons two whales with one right-and-left throw. The frigate rounds Cape Horn on July 6 and enters the Pacific. Every eye is on the sea. Aronnax barely leaves the deck, while Ned, still a skeptic, spends most of his time reading or sleeping. He points out that they are wandering "at random": if the creature ever existed, it is long gone.

The frigate crosses the Pacific to the seas off Japan, where the monster was last seen. For three months it chases every whale spout from Japan to America and finds nothing. The crew's excitement turns to shame and then fury at having been fooled by a fairy tale. Only Farragut's stubbornness keeps the ship there. Facing something close to mutiny, he asks for just three more days, after which he promises to head for home.

The deadline runs out on November 5, with the frigate less than 200 miles from Japan. That night Aronnax admits to Conseil that the whole business was foolish and that people will laugh at them; Conseil calmly agrees that it will serve master right. Before he can finish his sentence, Ned Land's voice rings out: "Ahoy! There's the thing in question, abreast of us to leeward!"

chapters.title: At Full Steam
chapters.summary: The glowing creature circles the frigate and outruns it through a full day's chase; a cannon shell bounces off its hide. That night Ned Land harpoons it while it lies still, the harpoon rings as if on something hard, and a violent collision throws Aronnax into the sea.
details: Under the water lies an intense, oval glow that Aronnax judges to be electric. It darts at the frigate, circles it at twice its speed, then suddenly goes out and reappears on the other side. Farragut retreats until daylight, calling it a gigantic, electric narwhal. Near midnight they hear a huge blast like a whale spouting, and Farragut confirms Ned has earned the $2,000 prize.

At dawn the creature surfaces as a long blackish body about 250 feet long, blowing two jets of water and steam. Aronnax classifies it as a cetacean. Farragut orders full steam, and the chase lasts all day. Each time the frigate speeds up, even with its valves overloaded to dangerous pressure, the animal matches it exactly. It lets Ned, perched under the bowsprit, get close and then darts away, and once it even circles the ship. A veteran gunner hits it with a cannon shell, but the shell bounces off. "That rascal must be covered with six-inch armor plate!" he says.

At nightfall the light reappears, and the creature seems to be asleep on the surface. The frigate creeps up silently. From the bobstays Ned hurls his harpoon from twenty feet away, and Aronnax hears it strike something hard. The light goes out, two huge waterspouts crash over the deck, and a terrible collision throws Aronnax overboard.

chapters.title: A Whale of Unknown Species
chapters.summary: Conseil jumps in after Aronnax, and the two swim for hours while the crippled frigate drifts away. Close to drowning, they are pulled onto the "monster" by Ned Land, and find it is a man-made submarine of riveted steel. At dawn masked crewmen haul them inside.
details: Aronnax surfaces in the dark and sees the frigate sailing away. Weighed down by his clothes, he is sinking when Conseil grabs him. Conseil jumped in deliberately ("being in master's employ, I followed master") and reports that the frigate's propeller and rudder were smashed, so it can no longer steer. He cuts away Aronnax's clothes with a knife, and the two take turns towing each other, hoping for the ship's longboats.

By one in the morning Aronnax is exhausted and Conseil is gasping. By moonlight they see the frigate five miles away, with no boats in sight. Then a voice answers Conseil's shouts. Aronnax collapses, bumps against something hard, and is hauled out of the water.

He comes to with Ned Land, who was also thrown overboard and climbed onto what he calls a floating islet: the narwhal itself. His harpoon was blunted because the beast is "made of boilerplate steel." Aronnax checks for himself. The back is smooth, rings like metal, and is held together by rivets. The monster that puzzled the world is a machine, an underwater boat built by human hands.

The boat starts moving west, driven by a propeller, and the three cling to a mooring ring as it speeds up. There is no hope of rescue by Farragut now. In lulls Aronnax thinks he hears faint music. At daybreak the hull begins to sink and Ned stamps and shouts at the crew to open up. A plate flies open, a man appears, gives a strange yell and vanishes. Then eight silent men with mask-like faces drag the three down inside.

chapters.title: "Mobilis in Mobili"
chapters.summary: The three are locked in a dark iron cell until two men visit: a stocky southern-looking man and a tall, commanding stranger. Neither seems to understand the story they tell in French, English, German and Latin. A silent steward brings clothes and a fine meal served on dishes marked with an N and the motto "Mobilis in Mobili."
details: The captives are shut in a pitch-black cell with iron walls, a table and some stools. Ned is ready to fight with his Bowie knife, while Conseil and Aronnax urge calm. After half an hour a ceiling globe floods the room with the same electric light they saw glowing around the "monster."

Two men enter. One is short, stocky and dark-haired, with the lively look of a man from Provence. The other is tall and pale, with black eyes, a calm and noble bearing and an extraordinarily wide, piercing gaze; Aronnax feels instinctively reassured by him. He seems to be the leader, and he speaks to his companion in a musical language Aronnax doesn't recognize.

Aronnax tells their story in French, Ned in angry English (complete with demands for habeas corpus and mimed hunger), Conseil in German and finally Aronnax in schoolboy Latin. The strangers listen politely but show no sign of understanding, and leave. Ned calls them rogues. Aronnax guesses that the commander and his chief officer were born in southern latitudes but can't place their nationality.

A steward, possibly deaf and mute, brings clothes of an unfamiliar fabric and lays an elegant meal of fish and dishes Aronnax can't identify, with water but no bread or wine. Every utensil bears a letter N inside the Latin motto "Mobilis in Mobili" ("moving within the moving element"), and Aronnax guesses N is the commander's initial. Ned and Conseil fall asleep at once. Aronnax lies awake, feeling the boat sink, before drifting into uneasy sleep.

chapters.title: The Tantrums of Ned Land
chapters.summary: The prisoners wake as the boat surfaces to renew its air, then wait hours without food. Ned talks of seizing the ship and grows more furious, and when the steward finally comes he throttles him, until a voice says in French: "Calm down, Mr. Land!"
details: Aronnax wakes first, short of breath because the air in the cell is used up. He wonders how the vessel renews its air. Then a fresh, salty breeze pours through a vent above the door and he feels the boat rolling: it has surfaced to breathe, like a whale. Ned realizes this explains the "bellowing" they heard from the Abraham Lincoln.

They seem to have slept about twenty-four hours, and they are starving. Ned jokes that their hosts may be fattening them up. Aronnax thinks they have stumbled on an important secret: if the crew value it above three lives, they are in danger; otherwise they will be set free. Conseil wonders if they might be made to join the crew. Ned proposes breaking out, then taking over the ship, since he guesses only about twenty men run it. Aronnax makes him promise not to lose his temper.

The hours drag on with no meal and no sound from the motionless boat. Ned paces like a caged animal and shouts at the walls, and Aronnax's good impression of the commander turns to dread that he is cruel and means to let them starve. When the steward finally opens the door, Ned throws him down and chokes him. As Conseil and Aronnax rush to pull him off, a voice speaks in French: "Calm down, Mr. Land! And you, professor, kindly listen to me!"

chapters.title: The Man of the Waters
chapters.summary: The commander reveals he speaks their languages and has decided their fate: they may live aboard his vessel in freedom of a sort but can never leave, since they now know his secret. He names himself Captain Nemo and his ship the Nautilus, and over a breakfast made entirely from the sea he speaks passionately of the ocean.
details: The speaker is the commander, the tall stranger from before. He says he speaks French, English, German and Latin fluently and had kept quiet to judge them; he knows exactly who they are. He reminds them that the Abraham Lincoln hunted him and shelled him, and that Ned harpooned him, so he could treat them as enemies, or simply set them back on the deck and dive. When Aronnax says that would be a savage's act, not a civilized man's, he flares up: he is not a civilized man, he has broken with society for reasons of his own, and he obeys none of its laws.

He has decided to let them stay aboard, free to move about, on one condition: when certain events require it, they must accept being confined to their cabins without question, so that they don't see what they aren't meant to see. They agree. But this freedom means never going home again, because they have stumbled on the secret of his whole existence. Ned refuses to promise not to escape, and the commander says he never asked him to. Then, more gently, he tells Aronnax he has read his book on the ocean depths, and invites him to join him as a fellow student on an underwater tour of the world, perhaps his last. Aronnax, the scientist, is deeply tempted.

Asked his name, the commander answers: to them he is simply Captain Nemo (Latin for "no one"), and they are passengers on the Nautilus. Ned and Conseil are taken off to eat, while Nemo leads Aronnax to an elegant dining room. Everything served comes from the sea: turtle loin that tastes like beef, dolphin liver, sea-cucumber preserves, cream from cetacean milk. Nemo explains that the sea also clothes him and supplies his perfumes, mattress, pens and ink.

He speaks of the sea with growing passion: it is life, movement and love, a place where a man is never lonely, and where tyrants' power stops thirty feet below the surface. "Here I recognize no superiors! Here I'm free!" He breaks off, recovers his icy calm, and offers to show Aronnax around the Nautilus.

chapters.title: The Nautilus
chapters.summary: Captain Nemo shows Aronnax the library of 12,000 books, a lounge filled with old-master paintings, music and a priceless collection of shells and pearls, and Aronnax's own stateroom next to the captain's bare, monk-like one.
details: Beyond the dining room is a library of 12,000 volumes in every language, including Aronnax's own book; it also serves as a smoking room. Nemo calls the books his last ties with dry land: he bought the final ones the day the Nautilus first submerged and has acted ever since as if humanity no longer thinks or writes. From a book published in 1865, Aronnax works out that Nemo can have lived underwater for three years at most. Nemo offers him cigars rolled from a nicotine-rich seaweed.

Next comes a large, brightly lit lounge that is really a museum: some thirty paintings by masters from Raphael and Leonardo to Delacroix, statues, and a piano-organ covered with sheet music by Mozart, Beethoven, Wagner and others. Nemo calls himself a collector, says these are his last mementos of shores now "dead" to him, and adds that he is himself dead, "quite as dead as those friends of yours sleeping six feet under." He then falls silent, lost in thought.

The lounge also holds Nemo's natural treasures, all gathered with his own hands: a fountain basin made from a giant clam shell, cases of coral and shells of enormous rarity and value, and pearls larger than any known to European collectors. Aronnax wonders how Nemo pays for all this. Nemo promises he may inspect every part of the ship, then shows him a comfortable stateroom in the bow next to his own. The captain's room is austere, with an iron bed and a worktable, and there Nemo sits Aronnax down to explain the ship's instruments.

chapters.title: Everything through Electricity
chapters.summary: Nemo explains that electricity, made from sodium he extracts from seawater, powers, lights and heats the Nautilus. He tours Aronnax through the ship's layout, the skiff it carries and the engine room, which can drive it at fifty miles an hour.
details: Nemo explains the instruments in his stateroom. Besides the usual compass, sextant, barometer and so on, there is a pressure gauge that tells the ship's depth and sounding lines that measure water temperature at different levels. Everything aboard runs on electricity, and he hints that his is not "the run-of-the-mill variety." He makes it from the sea itself: he extracts sodium from seawater, mixes it with mercury and uses it in place of zinc in his batteries (Bunsen cells). To extract the sodium he burns coal mined from the seafloor, which he says Aronnax will see him do.

Electricity lights the ship with a steady glow, runs a twenty-four-hour clock (since day and night no longer exist for him), shows the ship's speed, and works the pumps that store air in tanks, so the Nautilus can stay down as long as it wants. Aronnax says mankind will one day find this same power; Nemo icily replies that he is not so sure.

Aronnax describes the forward half of the ship (dining room, library, lounge, the two staterooms and the air tanks), divided by watertight bulkheads. Amidships a ladder leads to a watertight skiff fixed in a hollow in the hull. It can be released to rise to the surface, and it calls the Nautilus back by an electric wire. Further aft he passes Ned and Conseil finishing their meal, then the galley, where electricity cooks and distills drinking water, a bathroom, and the closed crew's quarters, which hide how many men are aboard.

In the engine room, at least twenty meters long, Bunsen cells feed huge electromagnets that turn a propeller six meters across, giving a top speed of fifty miles an hour. Aronnax can't see how electricity produces such power, but he accepts the results. When he asks how the ship dives, rises and holds its depth, Nemo hesitates, then agrees to explain, since Aronnax "will never leave this underwater boat."

chapters.title: Some Figures
chapters.summary: Over cigars in the lounge, Captain Nemo explains to Aronnax how the Nautilus is built, how it dives, steers and sees, and how he built it in secret. He ends by claiming to be infinitely rich.
details: Captain Nemo spreads out the Nautilus's plans and talks Aronnax through the figures. It is a seventy-meter cylinder with conical ends, built of two steel hulls joined by iron T-bars. Ballast tanks let it sink until it lies flush with the surface. Supplementary tanks take it deeper, and slanting side fins drive it down or up under the propeller's thrust. Because water barely compresses, little extra weight is needed to go deep, and pumps driven by electricity can empty the tanks against great pressure.

A helmsman steers from a pilothouse fitted with thick biconvex glass, and behind it a powerful electric beacon lights the sea for half a mile. Aronnax realizes the beacon explains the mysterious glow of the so-called narwhale. Nemo says ramming the Scotia was an accident. He attacked the Abraham Lincoln only in self-defence and left it able to reach port. He talks of his ship with a father's love: no rigging, no sails, no boilers, no storms below the waves.

Nemo says he studied in London, Paris and New York when he still lived on land. Each part of the Nautilus was ordered from a different maker under a different name, and he and his crew assembled it on a deserted islet, then burned every trace of their stay. With its collections the ship is worth four or five million francs. Asked if he is rich, Nemo says he could pay off France's ten-billion-franc national debt. Aronnax wonders whether he is being made a fool of.

chapters.title: The Black Current
chapters.summary: Nemo fixes the ship's position off Japan and the voyage officially begins on November 8. Then the lounge panels slide open, and Aronnax, Conseil and Ned Land watch the fish of the Black Current through the windows.
details: At noon the Nautilus surfaces, and from the platform Aronnax sees why it was taken for a sea creature: its plates overlap like reptile scales. Nemo takes the sun's altitude, then works out their position against the Paris meridian, an answer that tells Aronnax nothing about his nationality. They are about 300 miles off Japan, and Nemo declares that the voyage of underwater exploration begins on November 8. He sets a course east-northeast at fifty meters and leaves Aronnax the lounge and its charts.

Alone, Aronnax broods over the captain's hatred of humanity and the hand Nemo never offers. He traces on the map the Kuroshio, or Black Current, the warm ocean river they are about to cross. Ned Land and Conseil arrive and are stunned by the museum-like lounge. Ned wants to know how many crew there are and still talks of escape, calling the ship a sheet-iron prison where they will never see anything.

At that moment the lights go out, panels slide back, and two great windows open onto the sea, lit by the ship's beacon. Conseil lectures Ned on how fish are classified, and Ned rates each order by how good it is to eat. Then the fish arrive, and the two make a perfect naturalist between them: Ned names each fish, Conseil classifies it. Triggerfish, a rare Chinese ray, mackerel, moray eels and many more escort the ship for two hours. The panels close at five, and Aronnax sleeps as the Nautilus runs through the Black Current.

chapters.title: An Invitation in Writing
chapters.summary: Nemo disappears for days while the chief officer repeats a strange phrase on the platform each morning. Then a written note invites Aronnax and his companions to hunt in Nemo's forests on Crespo Island, and Nemo explains that the forests are underwater.
details: For days Captain Nemo does not appear. Aronnax studies the lounge's shells and pressed seaweeds, dresses in clothes woven from fan-mussel filaments, and begins his diary on paper made from eelgrass. Each morning, when the ship surfaces for air, the chief officer scans the horizon with a spyglass and calls down the hatch the same unintelligible phrase: "Nautron respoc lorni virch."

On November 16 Aronnax finds a note in an old-fashioned hand. Captain Nemo invites him and his companions to hunt the next morning in his forests on Crespo Island. Ned is delighted at the thought of solid ground, fresh venison and a chance to plan an escape. Aronnax finds Crespo on the map, a tiny rock in the north Pacific, and notes that Nemo only seems to visit desert islands.

Next morning Nemo, saying nothing of his eight-day absence, explains over breakfast that his forests are underwater. Aronnax briefly thinks he has gone mad. Nemo describes the gear that makes the trip possible: a Rouquayrol air tank refined to supply nine or ten hours of air under a copper helmet, a Ruhmkorff electric lamp at the belt, and air rifles that fire small glass capsules charged with electricity, fatal at the slightest touch. Convinced, Aronnax agrees, collects Ned and Conseil, and they go to the room where they will dress for the outing.

chapters.title: Strolling the Plains
chapters.summary: Ned refuses to put on a diving suit, but Aronnax and Conseil suit up and walk out onto the seafloor with Nemo and a powerful crewman. They cross sunlit plains of sand, beds of ooze and meadows of algae down to a depth of 100 meters, where Nemo points out the forest.
details: In the ship's arsenal and wardrobe, Ned Land learns the hunting grounds are underwater and refuses to wear a suit. Nobody forces him. Crewmen help Aronnax and Conseil into rubber suits with copper-mailed chests and lead-soled boots, and Captain Nemo and a herculean crewman suit up too. Aronnax inspects his rifle, which stores compressed air in its butt and holds some twenty electric bullets. With copper helmets screwed on and air tanks working, the four pass through a chamber that floods, and step out onto the bottom ten meters down.

Once in the water the gear loses most of its weight, and Aronnax moves freely. Sunlight reaches the bottom so strongly that he can see 100 meters. He crosses fine, mirror-like sand. Toward ten o'clock, slanting sunlight splits into rainbow colors along the edges of rocks, coral, anemones and shells. He cannot speak to Conseil through the helmets, while Nemo and his companion talk with hand signals, so Aronnax talks to himself and wastes air.

The ground changes to ooze, then to meadows of algae, with long ribbons of seaweed floating overhead. By noon the colors fade, and the floor slopes steeply down to 100 meters, where the light turns to a reddish twilight. Nemo stops and points to dark masses in the shadows: the forest of Crespo Island.

chapters.title: An Underwater Forest
chapters.summary: The party walks through the Crespo forest, goes deeper by lamplight to the foot of the island, and turns back without climbing ashore. On the way back they shoot a sea otter and an albatross and lie flat while two sharks pass over them.
details: In the forest every plant grows straight up toward the surface, and Aronnax keeps confusing plants with animals. Around one o'clock the party rests under the kelp, and the divers fall asleep. Aronnax wakes to find a meter-high sea spider about to spring at him, and Nemo's companion kills it with his rifle butt. Instead of turning back, Nemo leads them on and down to about 150 meters, where sunlight gives out and they switch on their lamps. Nemo raises his rifle several times but never fires.

At about four they reach a granite cliff: the base of Crespo Island, which is land. Nemo stops there and goes no farther. They return by a steeper route toward the surface. Nemo shoots a valuable sea otter, a rare animal whose fur would sell for a high price, and his companion brings down an albatross skimming the waves above them. In the shallows Aronnax sees their party reflected upside down on the underside of the surface.

Within sight of the Nautilus's beacon, Nemo suddenly throws Aronnax to the ground, and his companion does the same to Conseil. Two huge blue sharks glide past, glowing faintly. Their poor eyesight saves the divers. Half an hour later the party is back aboard, and an exhausted Aronnax goes to his cabin.

chapters.title: Four Thousand Leagues Under the Pacific
chapters.summary: Nemo talks about the ocean as a living thing, then mostly disappears as the Nautilus heads southeast past Hawaii and the Marquesas. In mid-December the travelers see a freshly sunk ship, the Florida, with its dead still on deck.
details: On November 18 some twenty crewmen haul in the nets. They are of several nationalities, all with European features, and speak only their strange language among themselves. Captain Nemo, seemingly half to himself, praises the ocean's circulation, its salts and its tiny animals, and imagines free underwater towns. Then he breaks off, perhaps at the thought of a tyrant. He asks Aronnax about known ocean depths and promises to show him deeper.

After that Nemo is rarely seen. The chief officer marks their position on the chart each day. Conseil has told Ned about the undersea walk, and Ned is sorry he missed it. The lounge panels open for hours almost daily. The ship crosses the Tropic of Cancer, passes Hawaii on November 27 after 4,860 leagues, crosses the equator on December 1 and sights Nuku Hiva in the Marquesas. On December 9–10 it runs for hours through a school of millions of migrating squid.

On December 11 the Nautilus is lying still 1,000 meters down when Conseil calls Aronnax to the window. A three-master hangs in the water, sinking, its masts cut away. Four sailors are lashed to the deck, one still at the wheel. A young woman is halfway out of a skylight, holding her child above her head. Sharks are already closing in. As the Nautilus circles, Aronnax reads the name on the stern: the Florida, of Sunderland, England.

chapters.title: Vanikoro
chapters.summary: The Nautilus crosses the South Pacific to Vanikoro, where the explorer La Pérouse's ships were wrecked. Nemo shows Aronnax the wreckage and reveals what became of the last survivors, with proof he found himself.
details: The Nautilus passes the coral islands of the Tuamotus, where Aronnax studies how coral polyps build reefs and atolls. When he says these islands may one day form a new continent, Nemo replies coldly that the earth needs new men, not new continents. The ship goes on past Tahiti, Tonga, Samoa and Fiji, where the crew feast on oysters, and through the New Hebrides at Christmas, which Ned misses keenly.

On December 27 Nemo reappears and names their position: Vanikoro, where the French navigator the Count de La Pérouse lost his two ships, the Compass and the Astrolabe, in the 1780s. At Nemo's request Aronnax recounts what is known. D'Entrecasteaux searched in vain. Captain Peter Dillon found the first relics in 1827. Dumont d'Urville raised anchors and cannon from the reef and put up a monument. The natives said the survivors built a smaller boat and sailed away, and no one knows where it was lost.

Through the lounge windows Nemo shows Aronnax coral-covered cannon, anchors and other wreckage. Then he tells him the rest: the survivors sailed for the Solomon Islands and died with all hands on the west coast of the main island. As proof he produces a tin box stamped with the arms of France. It holds La Pérouse's naval orders, with notes in the hand of King Louis XVI. Nemo calls this a fine death for a seaman, and hopes he and his companions will rest in no grave but a coral one.

chapters.title: The Torres Strait
chapters.summary: After New Year, the Nautilus threads the reefs of the Torres Strait and runs aground off Gueboroa Island. Nemo calmly waits for the full-moon tide and lets the three companions go ashore in the skiff.
details: On January 1, 1868, Conseil wishes Aronnax a happy new year. He says Ned longs for meat, bread, wine and escape, while he himself is happy to stay and see everything, so one of the two will be pleased whatever happens. The ship skirts the Great Barrier Reef, and Nemo announces they will reach the Indian Ocean through the Torres Strait, the narrow, reef-choked passage between Australia and New Guinea. Ned is glad: the route brings them nearer European seas.

With Nemo apparently steering, the Nautilus winds between the reefs on the surface. Ned says one brush with the coral would tear the hull apart. Near Gueboroa Island it strikes a reef and sticks fast at high tide. Nemo calls it "an incident," not an accident, and makes clear that nothing will make him set foot on land again. In five days the full moon will raise the tide enough to float them off, he says.

Ned thinks the ship is finished and wants to slip away, but Aronnax says escaping near New Guinea would be madness. Ned and Conseil beg for a trip ashore, and to Aronnax's surprise Nemo grants it at once and without asking for a promise to come back. On January 5, armed with rifles and axes, the three row the skiff through the reefs, Ned dreaming aloud of venison, and land on Gueboroa's beach.

chapters.title: Some Days Ashore
chapters.summary: On Gueboroa Island the three gather coconuts, breadfruit, bananas and sago and, on a second day, hunt pigeons, a bird of paradise, a wild pig and kangaroos. As they feast on the beach and talk of never going back, a stone lands at their feet.
details: On the first day Ned cracks coconuts and roasts breadfruit, which tastes like soft bread with a flavor of artichoke. He plans to ferment the pulp so it will keep aboard. The three gather bananas, jackfruit, mangoes, pineapples, palm cabbages, beans and yams, and Ned fells sago palms for their starchy flour. They return to a silent Nautilus where nobody appears.

On January 6 they go back. Wary kingfishers suggest that people visit the island often. Aronnax longs for a bird of paradise, but they waste their ammunition firing at the birds in flight. Conseil shoots a pigeon and a ringdove for lunch, then catches a rare "great emerald" bird of paradise by hand, because it is drunk on nutmeg. Aronnax explains how islanders fake these birds for European collectors. Ned finally gets his red meat: a wild pig, then a dozen small kangaroos.

At six they cook pork cutlets on the beach and feast with fruit, sago, breadfruit and fermented coconut liquor. Somewhat tipsy, Conseil wonders aloud about not returning to the Nautilus that evening, and Ned about never returning. At that moment a stone whizzes out of the forest and lands at their feet.

chapters.title: The Lightning Bolts of Captain Nemo
chapters.summary: Papuan islanders drive the three back to the ship and then surround the stranded Nautilus in growing numbers. Nemo is unconcerned, and when the hatches open at high tide, an electrified railing throws back the boarders as the ship floats free on time.
details: About twenty islanders with bows and slings attack, and the three escape in the skiff, Ned clutching his pig and kangaroos, with a hundred islanders wading after them. Aboard, they find Nemo lost in playing the organ. Unimpressed by the word "savages," he asks whether these people are any worse than men elsewhere and says the Nautilus has nothing to fear from them. Fires burn on the beach all night.

On January 8 some 500 or 600 islanders gather, crossing the exposed coral at low tide to come near the ship. Aronnax and Conseil dredge for shells, and Aronnax finds a rare treasure: an olive shell that coils the "wrong" way, left-handed. A sling stone shatters it in Conseil's hands. Conseil fires back and breaks an amulet bracelet on the thrower's arm. Aronnax tells him a shell is not worth a human life. Then dugout canoes surround the ship and arrows rain down.

Nemo, busy with calculations, has the hatches closed and says he wants no Papuan to die because of his visit. He praises Dumont d'Urville, who was nearly wrecked in this same strait, but answers icily when Aronnax says the Nautilus has run aground like d'Urville's ships. It will float off, he says, tomorrow at 2:40. That night the islanders stamp across the platform. Next afternoon the crew open the hatches. Each islander who grabs the companionway railing is hurled back in terror, and so is Ned, who cries that he has been struck by lightning. The railing is charged with the ship's electricity. At 2:40 exactly the tide lifts the Nautilus off and it leaves the Torres Strait.

chapters.title: “Aegri Somnia”
chapters.summary: The Nautilus heads west past Timor into the Indian Ocean while Nemo runs experiments on sea temperature and density. On January 18 something on the horizon throws him into a rage. The three companions are locked in their old cell and drugged to sleep.
details: The ship races west past Timor and into the open Indian Ocean. Nemo takes the Nautilus as deep as 10,000 meters to measure water temperatures himself and finds a constant 4.5 degrees centigrade at 1,000 meters. Aronnax wonders who these findings are for, since they seem bound to die with Nemo. When Nemo lists the densities of different seas, he mentions the Mediterranean, the Ionian and the Adriatic, and Aronnax concludes the ship does visit European waters.

On January 16, drifting with its beacon off, the Nautilus enters a dazzling stretch of phosphorescent water, alive with tiny glowing animals, where porpoises and sailfish play. Aronnax notes how the three have grown used to the life aboard, "at home in our shell" like snails.

On January 18, in rough weather, the chief officer calls out a different phrase. Nemo examines the horizon with growing tension and argues with his excited officer, then orders more speed. When Aronnax raises his own telescope, Nemo snatches it away, his face twisted with hatred. He is staring at the horizon, not at Aronnax. Invoking one of their agreements, he has the three companions locked in the cell where they spent their first night. After lunch the light goes out, and all three fall into a drugged sleep. Before he goes under, Aronnax hears the hatches close and feels the ship dive.

chapters.title: The Coral Realm
chapters.summary: Aronnax wakes free in his cabin, and a haggard Nemo asks him to treat a crewman with a terrible head wound, who dies in the night. The next day the three companions follow Nemo and his crew to a coral forest on the seafloor and watch the man's burial in a hidden cemetery.
details: Aronnax wakes in his own stateroom, free, with no memory of the night. Ned and Conseil know no more than he does. In the afternoon Nemo appears, exhausted and red-eyed, and asks whether Aronnax is a physician. He is, and Nemo takes him to a cabin near the crew's quarters. There a man of about forty, with English features, lies with his skull smashed open. Nemo says that in a collision an engine lever cracked, and this man threw himself in front of the chief officer to take the blow. A brother dies for his brother, Nemo says; that is the law on board. Aronnax says the man will be dead in two hours, and Nemo weeps. That night Aronnax hears something like a funeral chant.

In the morning Nemo invites the three on an undersea walk, and this time Ned comes too. With a dozen crewmen they walk into a coral realm: thickets of precious red coral whose polyps pull back at a touch, then dark galleries that slope down to about 300 meters, the depth at which coral stops growing, where the coral rises like a huge stone forest.

In a clearing stands a cross of coral among low mounds laid out by human hands. Four crewmen carry an oblong bundle. Aronnax realizes this is a cemetery, and they have brought the dead man's body. A grave is dug, the body, wrapped in fan-mussel cloth, is lowered in, and Nemo and his men kneel in prayer and farewell. Back on the platform Nemo, holding back sobs, says their dead lie here forgotten by the world but not by them, and the coral will seal them in. When Aronnax says at least the dead are safe from sharks, Nemo answers: "of sharks and men!"

chapters.title: The Indian Ocean
chapters.summary: Aronnax broods over what Captain Nemo might really be as the Nautilus heads west across the Indian Ocean. Ned Land presses to escape near India, but Aronnax wants to stay aboard until they reach European waters.
details: The Second Part opens with Aronnax taking stock. Conseil still sees Captain Nemo as a misunderstood genius who has turned his back on the world. Aronnax is no longer satisfied with that. The night they were drugged and locked up, the spyglass snatched from his hands and the crewman fatally hurt in an unexplained collision all suggest something darker: perhaps the Nautilus serves some scheme of revenge. The three men are prisoners in all but name, bound by no promise. Yet Aronnax admits he wants to finish this tour of the world's seas before he leaves, even at some risk.

On 21 January 1868 the Nautilus sets course due west. Aronnax tests the chief officer with loud remarks in French and decides the man does not understand the language. Days pass in study: seabirds, turtles, armored trunkfish, puffers and archerfish. The ship passes Keeling Island and turns northwest toward the tip of India.

Ned Land sees roads, railways and fellow Europeans ahead and argues that the time has come to slip away. Aronnax refuses to be drawn. The ship is heading back toward Europe, he says, so let it carry them there first. Privately, he means to make the most of his luck in being aboard.

The sights continue. A fleet of argonauts sails on the surface with their arms spread like sails, then vanishes at once. Conseil remarks that, like Captain Nemo, the argonaut could leave its shell but never does. Sharks escort the ship and enrage Ned. At the mouth of the Bay of Bengal they pass corpses carried down by the Ganges, and that night the Nautilus crosses a 'milk sea', water turned white by countless tiny glowing organisms.

chapters.title: A New Proposition from Captain Nemo
chapters.summary: Off Ceylon, Captain Nemo invites Aronnax and his companions to walk the pearl beds of the Gulf of Mannar, casually mentioning sharks. Aronnax spends the evening dreading the outing while explaining pearls to Ned and Conseil, both of whom cheerfully agree to go.
details: On 28 January the Nautilus lies off Ceylon. Captain Nemo offers to show Aronnax the pearl fisheries of the Gulf of Mannar. The harvest has not started, so there will be no fishermen. Nemo describes the divers' hard lives: they plunge with a stone between their feet, last about thirty seconds underwater, ruin their health, and earn a penny for each oyster that holds a pearl. Then, as he leaves, he asks lightly whether the professor is afraid of sharks, and says they may hunt one or two.

Aronnax is horrified, and hopes Conseil will refuse so that he has an excuse to stay behind. Instead Ned and Conseil arrive delighted. Nemo has invited them in the friendliest terms and said nothing about sharks. Unsure how to warn them, Aronnax gives a lecture on pearls instead: how they form around a grain of sand inside an oyster, how they are harvested, sorted through sieves and priced, and what famous pearls have been worth.

The talk turns comic. Aronnax keeps saying 'sharks' when he means pearls or francs. Ned tells of the cheap pearl necklace he bought for his fiancée, Kate Tender, who married someone else. Aronnax laughs that the pearls were glass beads. He then reckons the great pearl in Nemo's collection is worth two million francs. Ned muses that bringing such a pearl home would make their story more believable. When Aronnax finally asks, in Nemo's offhand tone, whether they fear sharks, Ned boasts that he is a professional harpooner. Conseil quietly says that if his master faces sharks, he will face them too.

chapters.title: A Pearl Worth Ten Million
chapters.summary: On the Mannar pearl bank, Captain Nemo shows Aronnax a gigantic clam hiding an enormous pearl, then saves an Indian diver from a shark and is himself saved by Ned Land's harpoon. He gives the stunned fisherman a bag of pearls.
details: Before dawn the skiff carries Nemo, Aronnax, Ned and Conseil toward Mannar Island. They put on diving suits but take no lamps, which might attract dangerous creatures, and no rifles, only daggers; Ned brings his harpoon. Underwater, Aronnax's fears fade. They cross fields of fish, crabs and shellfish to the oyster bank, where Ned greedily fills a net.

Nemo leads them into a cave to a giant clam over two meters wide. He wedges it open with his dagger and lifts the flesh to show a loose pearl as big as a coconut. Aronnax reaches for it, but Nemo stops him and lets the shell close. He is plainly leaving the pearl to grow, perhaps for his museum. Aronnax values it at ten million francs or more.

They then watch, hidden, as a lone Indian diver works the bank before the season. A huge shark strikes him down. Nemo rises and fights the shark at close quarters with his dagger. When he is knocked to the seafloor and the jaws open over him, Ned Land drives his harpoon into its heart. Nemo cuts the diver free of his stone and carries him up to his boat. Once the man is revived, Nemo gives him a bag of pearls, and the man stares at the four copper-headed figures in bewilderment.

Back in the skiff Nemo thanks Ned, who answers that he owed it to him. A swarm of sharks devours the carcass. Aboard the Nautilus, Aronnax is struck by Nemo's courage and by his care for a fellow human. When he says so, Nemo replies with feeling that the Indian lives in the land of the oppressed, and that he himself is, and will be until his last breath, a native of that same land.

chapters.title: The Red Sea
chapters.summary: The Nautilus heads up past Arabia and into the Red Sea, apparently a dead end. Captain Nemo then reveals that he has found an underground passage, the Arabian Tunnel, through which he will take them to the Mediterranean.
details: Leaving Ceylon, the Nautilus has covered some 7,500 leagues since Japan. When it heads for the Gulf of Oman, Ned complains that the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea are both blind alleys. Aronnax guesses the ship will turn back and round the Cape of Good Hope. Ned reminds him they have been prisoners for nearly three months. Aronnax, absorbed in the voyage, will discuss escape only if a real chance arises, and notes that he is coming to sound like Nemo.

The ship passes Muscat and Aden, slips through the Strait of Bab el Mandeb underwater to avoid heavy steamer traffic, and enters the Red Sea. Aronnax spends happy hours at the windows studying coral, sponges and fish.

On 9 February Nemo joins him on the platform and talks knowledgeably about the sea's dangerous reputation, the origin of its name, the Israelites' crossing and the old canals linking the Nile to the Red Sea. When Aronnax says it would be a shame for the Nautilus's secret to die with its inventor, Nemo is silent. He speaks with surprising warmth in praise of Ferdinand de Lesseps and the Suez Canal.

Then he says they will be in the Mediterranean in two days. Aronnax is astonished. Nemo explains that nature long ago cut a passage under the isthmus, which he calls the Arabian Tunnel. He found it by noticing identical fish in both seas, then tagging fish near Suez with copper rings and catching some later off Syria. When Aronnax asks how he discovered it, Nemo answers that there can be no secrets between men who will never leave each other.

chapters.title: Arabian Tunnel
chapters.summary: Ned Land harpoons a huge dugong in a dangerous chase near the Arabian coast. That night Captain Nemo brings Aronnax into the wheelhouse as he steers the Nautilus through the Arabian Tunnel into the Mediterranean in under twenty minutes.
details: Conseil is delighted by the news of the tunnel; Ned scoffs. On 10 February Ned spots a dark shape in the water, which Conseil takes for a mermaid. Aronnax identifies it as a dugong, a rare sea mammal. Ned is wild to hunt it. Nemo gives permission, saying its meat is excellent and warning him to aim well.

Ned, Aronnax and Conseil set out in the skiff with silent crewmen at the oars. Ned's first throw only wounds the animal, and they chase it for an hour. Then the dugong turns and charges, half swamping the boat and lifting it in its teeth. Ned stabs it again and again until he pierces its heart. The carcass weighs 5,000 kilograms, and Aronnax finds its meat better than veal.

The ship moves slowly up the Gulf of Suez, past Mount Sinai and the bay of El Tur, whose waters do look red as Nemo said. Near Suez, Nemo invites Aronnax into the wheelhouse, a small glass-windowed cabin at the end of the platform. For an hour they follow a rock wall. Then Nemo takes the wheel himself and the Nautilus enters a dark gallery. The current sweeps it through like an arrow, despite the engines running in reverse. At 10:35 Nemo turns and says simply, 'The Mediterranean.'

chapters.title: The Greek Islands
chapters.summary: In the Mediterranean, Ned Land forces Aronnax to agree that they will escape at the first real chance. Among the Greek islands Aronnax watches Captain Nemo signal to a diver and send off a chest of gold, and then the captain takes the Nautilus into a boiling underwater eruption off Santorini.
details: On 12 February the Nautilus surfaces off Port Said. Ned is finally convinced, and says they must leave now that they are in Europe. Aronnax is torn, because he is rewriting his book on the ocean depths and has no wish to go. Conseil declares himself neutral. Ned asks whether Aronnax would refuse freedom if Nemo offered it once and never again, and Aronnax cannot answer. In the end he concedes that Nemo will never free them, so they must take their first good chance. That chance must be certain, since a failed attempt would not be forgiven. Ned plans to swim for it near a coast or take the skiff. Aronnax predicts Nemo will keep well clear of land.

For a while he seems right. The ship stays deep and far from shore. On 14 February, near Crete, Nemo is silent and preoccupied and watches the sea through the open panels. A diver swims up to the window. Nemo signals to him, and the man swims away. Nemo explains that he is Nicolas of Cape Matapan, nicknamed 'Il Pesce' (the Fish), a famous diver of the Cyclades. Then, ignoring Aronnax, Nemo fills an iron-bound chest with gold ingots worth about five million francs and writes an address on it in what looks like modern Greek. That night the skiff goes out and returns two hours later. Aronnax and his friends wonder where the gold came from and who received it.

The next day the lounge grows unbearably hot. Nemo explains that they are in boiling water near Santorini, between the volcanic islets of Nea Kameni and Palea Kameni. He has brought Aronnax to see an underwater eruption, and describes the new islands he watched rise there in 1866. The sea turns white, then red with iron salts, flames glare and sulfur fumes seep into the lounge until Nemo withdraws. Aronnax reflects that an escape attempt in these waters would have been fatal. On 16 February the ship rounds Cape Matapan and leaves the Greek islands.

chapters.title: The Mediterranean in Forty-Eight Hours
chapters.summary: Captain Nemo races the Nautilus across the Mediterranean in two days, staying deep and out of sight, which leaves Ned no chance to escape. Aronnax glimpses fish and sea creatures in passing and sees a graveyard of wrecks before the ship rides an undercurrent out through Gibraltar.
details: The Nautilus crosses some 600 leagues of Mediterranean between the morning of 16 February and sunrise on the 18th. Nemo never appears. Aronnax senses that this sea, hemmed in by coasts, brings back memories or regrets the captain would rather avoid. The ship surfaces only at night, and at such speed Ned has no hope of using the skiff.

Aronnax sorts the fish into those he saw, those he glimpsed and those he missed altogether. He watches lampreys, rays, sharks, sturgeons and racing schools of tuna. In the shallows of the Strait of Sicily the ship slows, and Conseil busily catalogs mollusks and crustaceans. He and Aronnax discuss the ridge that once joined Europe to Africa, and Aronnax remarks that the earth is slowly cooling. Conseil concludes there is plenty of time to finish the voyage, 'if Ned Land doesn't mess things up.'

In the western basin the ship runs deep through a field of shipwrecks: hulls upright with rigging intact, overturned steamers, scattered anchors and cannons, which grow thicker near Gibraltar. One wrecked steamer makes Aronnax wonder about the many lives lost. Early on 18 February the Nautilus uses a deep countercurrent that carries Mediterranean water out to the ocean, glimpses the sunken ruins of the Temple of Hercules, and emerges into the Atlantic.

chapters.title: The Bay of Vigo
chapters.summary: Off Spain, Ned Land sets an escape for nine o'clock that night, but just before the hour the Nautilus stops in the Bay of Vigo. There Captain Nemo shows Aronnax his crew gathering treasure from sunken Spanish galleons, and hints that he uses his wealth for the oppressed.
details: In the Atlantic, Ned follows Aronnax to his stateroom and announces that they will escape that very evening. They will be a few miles off Spain, the night will be cloudy, and the wind is blowing toward shore. He and Conseil will go to the central companionway, and Aronnax is to wait in the library for his signal. Ned has stowed provisions in the skiff and has a wrench for its bolts. Aronnax, who gave his word, cannot refuse.

He spends an agonizing day torn between freedom and regret at leaving the Nautilus and its unexplored Atlantic. He wonders how Nemo will take their flight, and begins to suspect that the captain keeps up some link with the shore and perhaps leaves the ship himself. Visiting the lounge one last time, he finds Nemo's door ajar. On the wall are portraits of men devoted to freedom and to oppressed peoples: Kosciusko, Botzaris, O'Connell, Washington, Manin, Lincoln and John Brown. He wonders whether Nemo is a fighter for oppressed races. The clock strikes eight and he hurries out.

Just before nine, waiting at his post, he feels the Nautilus stop and settle on the bottom. Nemo enters and tells him the history of a treasure fleet. In 1702 Spanish galleons laden with American gold and silver sheltered in the Bay of Vigo, and when an English fleet attacked, their French escort burned and sank them. They are now in that very bay. Through the windows Aronnax sees divers from the crew hauling up gold, silver and jewels from rotting chests. This is where Nemo's millions come from, along with a thousand other wreck sites he has charted.

When Aronnax regrets that such wealth will help none of the poor, Nemo flares up. Does Aronnax think he is unaware of suffering people and oppressed races, 'poor people to comfort, victims to avenge'? He breaks off, as if he has said too much. Aronnax now guesses that the gold sent off near Crete went to the island's rebels against Ottoman rule.

chapters.title: A Lost Continent
chapters.summary: With the Nautilus heading away from Europe, Ned's escape is off. That night Captain Nemo takes Aronnax alone on a long walk across the dark Atlantic floor, up a mountain lit by an underwater volcano, to the ruins of Atlantis.
details: On 19 February Ned is bitterly disappointed. Aronnax explains the night's events and half hopes Ned will give up the idea of escape, but Ned only wishes he had gathered some treasure himself and vows to try again. By noon the ship is 150 leagues from land, heading south-southwest. Escape is out of the question, and Aronnax feels secretly relieved.

Near eleven that night Nemo invites Aronnax on a night walk, without Ned, Conseil or any crewman, and without lamps. On the seafloor 300 meters down, a reddish glow two miles off lights their way. They cross slimy plains where Aronnax hears rain drumming on the surface far above and feels bones crunch underfoot. Strangely regular piles of stone lie in rows. They climb through a forest of petrified trees, past caves where giant crustaceans watch from the dark, to a plateau of ruined palaces and temples.

From the summit Aronnax sees that the mountain is a volcano pouring lava into the sea, and below it lies a ruined city with temples, an aqueduct, an acropolis and a harbor. Unable to speak through his helmet, he is desperate to know where he is. Nemo picks up a piece of chalky stone and writes one word on a black rock: ATLANTIS.

Aronnax recalls Plato's account of the vast continent, told to Solon by Egyptian priests, that warred with ancient Athens and was swallowed in a day and a night. He longs to explore it all. Nemo leans motionless on a mossy monument as if lost in thought, and Aronnax wonders whether he comes here to live among the past, having no wish for the present. After an hour, under a brief gleam of moonlight, they walk back to the Nautilus and arrive at dawn.

chapters.title: The Underwater Coalfields
chapters.summary: The Nautilus skims over Atlantis and then enters an extinct volcano through an underwater channel. Captain Nemo explains that this hidden harbor is where his men mine coal to make the sodium that powers the ship, and while it reloads Aronnax, Ned and Conseil explore the cavern.
details: On 20 February the Nautilus runs south a few meters above the plains of Atlantis. Aronnax tells Conseil the story of the Atlanteans, but Conseil is too busy classifying fish to listen. Toward evening a high wall blocks the way south. Their position has not been marked on the chart, perhaps on purpose.

Next morning Aronnax climbs onto the platform into total darkness. Nemo tells him they are underground. When the beacon comes on, he sees the ship moored by a wharf-like bank on a lake inside a huge hollow mountain, with daylight showing through the crater far above. Nemo explains that this is an extinct volcano flooded by the sea, entered by a channel ten meters below the surface: a secret, storm-proof home port. Here prehistoric forests have turned to coal under the sea. His men mine it in diving suits to make the sodium for his batteries, and the smoke from the crater makes the mountain look like a live volcano. This time they will only load stored sodium and leave after one day.

Aronnax, Ned and Conseil walk the inner beach and climb the volcanic slopes. Ned is looking for a way out, but the walls overhang near the top. They find violets, a bees' nest from which Ned takes honey to make cake, and birds of prey. Ned brings down a bustard with a stone. Resting in a cave, Aronnax tells Ned he hopes the ship will now head back toward the coasts of Europe and America, giving him a better chance. They doze off and are woken by Conseil as the rising tide floods in.
Back aboard, the loading is finished. Nemo waits, perhaps for nightfall, and by the next day the Nautilus is out again in the Atlantic.

chapters.title: The Sargasso Sea
chapters.summary: The Nautilus crosses the weed-choked Sargasso Sea and then races south through the Atlantic for weeks, dimming hopes of escape. On 13 March Captain Nemo takes it down to a record depth of 16,000 meters, where he photographs the bare rocks of the ocean floor.
details: Heading south, the Nautilus passes under the Sargasso Sea, a still basin ringed by the Gulf Stream and matted with floating gulfweed and wreckage. Aronnax explains, following Maury, why the weed collects there. From 23 February to 12 March the ship runs steadily down the middle of the Atlantic. Aronnax guesses Nemo means to round Cape Horn and return to the Pacific.

Escape is impossible in these empty seas. Aronnax wonders about asking Nemo outright to free them in exchange for their word of silence, but fears that raising the subject might make the captain suspicious. He sees little of Nemo. In the library he finds his own book on the ocean depths with Nemo's notes in the margins, sometimes correcting him, and at night he hears the captain playing melancholy music on the organ. Once a whaler's boats chase the Nautilus as if it were a whale; Nemo simply dives, and Ned is sorry the whalers could not harpoon it. Aronnax notes sharks, dolphins hunting flying fish, and other sea life.

On 13 March, nearly 13,000 leagues from their starting point, Nemo decides to test deep soundings that others have failed to finish. Using its slanting fins and full power, the Nautilus dives at an angle. Fish thin out and disappear. The hull groans and the windows seem to bow under the pressure. Captain and professor discuss how life can survive in the deep. At 16,000 meters, four vertical leagues down, they have passed beyond all life. Nemo has a camera brought in and takes a photograph of the black, polished rocks. Then he warns Aronnax to hold on, and the ship shoots back to the surface in four minutes, leaping clear of the water like a flying fish.

chapters.title: Sperm Whales and Baleen Whales
chapters.summary: The Nautilus heads past Cape Horn toward the south polar seas, and Ned grows sullen. Captain Nemo refuses to let Ned hunt a herd of harmless southern right whales, then uses the Nautilus's spur to slaughter a pack of attacking sperm whales, and Ned's resentment of Nemo deepens.
details: Instead of turning west into the Pacific at Cape Horn, the Nautilus keeps going south, perhaps toward the pole. Ned has grown silent and sullen, and his eyes burn whenever he meets the captain. He and Conseil ask Aronnax how many men are aboard. Aronnax calculates that the ship's air could support 625 men for a day, though he is sure they number far fewer. Conseil counsels resignation and hopes the ice will force Nemo back north. Privately he tells Aronnax that Ned is homesick and has nothing to occupy him.

On 14 March Ned sights a herd of southern right whales and is beside himself with longing. He trades tall tales with Aronnax about whales big enough to be mistaken for islands, whales that live a thousand years, and whales that sink ships. He then runs to ask Nemo for permission to hunt. Nemo refuses. These whales are harmless, the ship needs no oil, and killing for the sake of killing is a 'murderous pastime' that whalers practice. The dugong, he points out, was fresh meat for the crew. Ned turns away whistling 'Yankee Doodle'.

But Nemo points out a pack of sperm whales, 'merely mouth and teeth', about to attack the right whales, and says they deserve to be exterminated. He takes the helm and turns the Nautilus into a giant harpoon. For an hour it rams and slices through the sperm whales, untouched by their blows, while Ned cheers at the windows. When they surface, the sea is red for miles with mangled bodies.

Ned, his enthusiasm gone, calls it butchery; he is a hunter, not a butcher, and prefers his harpoon. Nemo replies, 'To each his own,' with a long look at him. Nemo's crew draws milk from a dead right whale, still with its calf beside it, and Aronnax finds it as good as cow's milk. From that day he notices Ned's hostility toward Nemo growing worse and resolves to keep a close watch on him.

chapters.title: The Ice Bank
chapters.summary: Captain Nemo forces the Nautilus through the Antarctic ice until it is stopped dead by the Ice Bank, then announces he will reach the South Pole by passing beneath it. After a tense day of bumping against the ice ceiling, the ship breaks into open water.
details: Heading south along the 50th meridian in mid-March, the Nautilus meets floating ice, then icebergs and whole fields of it. Ned Land knows such sights from Arctic fishing; Aronnax and Conseil are seeing them for the first time. Nemo stands on the platform and threads the ship through narrow channels, and when the ice closes in he drives the Nautilus into it like a battering ram. Compasses go wild near the magnetic pole, and snow has to be chipped off the hull with picks.

On March 18 the ship meets the Ice Bank, an unbroken wall of ice mountains, and freezes in place. Ned says no captain can beat nature. Nemo calmly tells Aronnax he will go on to the pole, not over the ice but under it. Aronnax catches fire with the idea and ends up arguing for it more boldly than Nemo, who is quietly amused. Conseil answers with his usual "As master wishes"; Ned shrugs, says they will never come back, and shuts himself in his cabin.

The air tanks are filled, crewmen chip the hull free, and the Nautilus dives to 800 meters and runs south under the ice at express-train speed. Next morning it tries to surface and strikes the ice ceiling, thousands of feet thick. All day it tries again. The air goes unrenewed, and Aronnax sleeps badly. By early on March 19 the ice has thinned, and at six o'clock Nemo appears at the lounge door: "Open sea!"

chapters.title: The South Pole
chapters.summary: Beyond the ice lies open sea and a volcanic polar shore teeming with birds and seals. After two days of cloud, Nemo fixes the sun at noon on the equinox, declares that they stand at the South Pole, and claims it in his own name under a black flag.
details: The sea beyond the Ice Bank is almost mild, crowded with birds and fish. The Nautilus finds an islet and a larger shore beyond it. Aronnax insists that Nemo be the first to step onto ground no human has touched; Nemo climbs a rock and stands there motionless, as if taking possession. The land is volcanic, smoking in places, with lichens, shellfish, auks, petrels and burrows full of penguins. Ned stays aboard, sulking. Fog hides the sun at noon, so no position can be taken.

The next day Aronnax and Conseil explore alone among herds of seals and walruses that have never met man. Aronnax lectures; Conseil classifies, and is glad Ned isn't there to start harpooning. Again the noon sun stays hidden. Nemo explains that tomorrow, March 21, is the equinox, the sun's last day above the horizon for six months. If it shows at noon cut exactly in half by the horizon, they are at the pole.

On March 21 the sky clears. Nemo, Aronnax and two crewmen climb a high peak, Aronnax holding the chronometer. At noon the sun's disk is cut in half: "The South Pole!" Nemo recites the explorers who tried and fell short, then claims this sixth of the world in his own name, unfurls a black flag with a gold N, and bids the sun farewell.

chapters.title: Accident or Incident?
chapters.summary: Heading north under the Ice Bank, the Nautilus is knocked over by a capsizing iceberg and wedged in a tunnel of ice. Both ends of the tunnel turn out to be blocked, and the ship is trapped.
details: On March 22 the Nautilus dives and heads north beneath the Ice Bank. Aronnax, writing up his notes, counts 14,000 leagues and runs through the voyage's wonders so far. At three in the morning a violent jolt throws him from his bed. The ship lies on its side at 360 meters. A grim Nemo tells him that this time it is "an accident," not an incident: an iceberg has turned over, and a block of ice has lifted the ship and tilted it.

Pumping out ballast, the Nautilus rights itself and stops just short of the ice ceiling. When the panels open, the three companions see they are floating in a narrow tunnel of ice, walls above, below and on both sides, all glittering like a mine of gems in the beacon's light. When the ship speeds up, the glare blinds them. Conseil says the civilized world will never be good enough for them now; Ned answers that they will never see it again.

At five o'clock the bow hits ice and the ship backs up, looking for the other exit. Aronnax, pretending to be calm, reads a book without noticing it is his own. At 8:25 the stern strikes ice too. Nemo confirms it: the overturned iceberg has closed every exit. They are boxed in.

chapters.title: Shortage of Air
chapters.summary: With air for only two days, Nemo's crew and the three captives dig in shifts through the ice floor while the water around them threatens to freeze solid. Close to suffocating, they finally crush through the last layer with the ship's weight, and the Nautilus rams up through the surface ice into open air.
details: Nemo coolly sets out the choices: death by crushing or by suffocation. The air tanks hold two days' supply, and the ship's air already needs renewing. Borings show that the ice beneath them is ten meters thick, so the crew begins cutting a trench the shape of the ship's outline. Ned volunteers with a pick, and Aronnax and Conseil take shifts too, breathing clean air from their diving tanks while the air inside the ship turns foul. At one meter per twelve hours, the job will outlast the air.

Then a worse danger: the water around the ship begins to freeze and the walls close in, threatening to crack the hull. Nemo has the ship's water heater pump boiling water out into the ice tunnel, which keeps the water just above freezing. Meanwhile the air on board grows nearly unbreathable. Conseil, holding Aronnax's hand, wishes he didn't have to breathe so there would be more air for master. Every man, Nemo included, gives up his air tank strictly at the end of his shift.

On the sixth day, with a meter of ice left, Nemo settles the ship into the trench and floods its tanks. The extra weight cracks the ice, and the Nautilus drops through and races north under the Ice Bank. Aronnax passes out and is dying when Ned and Conseil revive him with the last air in a diving tank, going without themselves. Twenty feet from the surface, the Nautilus tilts its spur upward and rams the ice again and again until it breaks through, and fresh air floods in.

chapters.title: From Cape Horn to the Amazon
chapters.summary: Recovered, the three companions are relieved to find the Nautilus heading north up the Atlantic past South America. Nemo stays out of sight while the ship races along the coast to the mouth of the Amazon, where Conseil is stunned by an electric ray.
details: On the platform the three gulp fresh air. Aronnax thanks Ned and Conseil for saving his life; Ned shrugs it off as simple arithmetic and says Aronnax can repay him by coming along when he escapes. By March 31 they round Cape Horn, and the positions the chief officer marks on the chart show, to Aronnax's relief, that they are going up the Atlantic rather than back into the empty Pacific. Nemo no longer appears.

The ship passes Tierra del Fuego and the Falkland Islands and runs north along the coast, through forests of giant seaweed and swarms of jellyfish. It flashes past Brazil at great speed, as Nemo seems to avoid crowded shores, much to Ned's annoyance. Then it explores a deep underwater valley that Nemo has charted himself. Off the Amazon, French Guiana is only twenty miles away, but the sea is too rough for the skiff, and Ned says nothing.

The trawl brings up a flood of specimens. Conseil grabs a flat ray that knocks him onto his back: an electric ray. Half-paralyzed, he still recites its classification, then takes his revenge by eating it, though it tastes like leather. The crew hunts manatees for meat and uses suckerfish on lines to catch sea turtles before the Nautilus heads back out to sea.

chapters.title: The Devilfish
chapters.summary: In the Caribbean, giant squid attack the Nautilus and jam its propeller. In the fight on the platform a crewman is carried off, crying for help in French, and Nemo saves Ned Land's life before weeping for his lost man.
details: The Nautilus keeps clear of the busy Caribbean islands, to Ned's disappointment. Six months into their captivity, he wants Aronnax to ask Nemo outright whether they will ever be freed. Aronnax holds back. Nemo has grown gloomy and withdrawn and seems to avoid him, and Aronnax wants his own research to reach the world someday.

Off the Bahamas, Conseil, Ned and Aronnax debate legends of giant squid, from the bishop who said mass on a squid he took for a rock to the gunboat Alecto, which in 1861 tore the tail off a real one. Conseil, peering through the window, calmly describes the creature point by point. An eight-meter squid is right outside, soon joined by six more.

The ship jolts to a stop: a squid's jaws are tangled in the propeller. Nemo surfaces to fight them with axes, and Ned joins in with his harpoon. The moment the hatch opens, tentacles pour in. One seizes a crewman, who screams "Help!" in French, the first sign to Aronnax that a fellow Frenchman is on board. Nemo hacks off seven of the arms, but the squid squirts ink and vanishes with the man.

In the bloody melee Ned is knocked down beneath a squid's open beak. Nemo drives his ax between its jaws, and Ned finishes it with a harpoon to the heart. "Tit for tat," Nemo tells him; he owed it to himself. Afterward Nemo stands by the beacon, covered in blood, weeping as he stares at the sea that took his companion.

chapters.title: The Gulf Stream
chapters.summary: Grieving, Nemo lets the Nautilus drift, then follows the Gulf Stream north. When Aronnax asks him on the three companions' behalf to free them, Nemo refuses outright, then rides out a hurricane on the surface off Long Island.
details: Nemo shuts himself away. It is the second crewman he has lost since the captives came aboard, and this one will not lie in the coral cemetery. Aronnax keeps thinking of the dead man's cry in French. For ten days the ship drifts aimlessly. On May 1 it joins the Gulf Stream, which Aronnax describes as a warm, salty river running through the ocean, and heads north past the Carolinas.

Off America the shore is close and the sea full of ships, but storms make the skiff useless. Ned, desperately homesick for Quebec and the St. Lawrence, insists that Aronnax confront Nemo today. Aronnax finds him at work on a manuscript in several languages, his research and his life story, signed with his name. It will be sealed in a floating case and thrown into the sea by the last man left alive on the Nautilus.

Aronnax offers to carry the manuscript himself if they are set free, and asks whether Nemo means to keep them forever. Nemo repeats what he said seven months before: whoever boards the Nautilus must never leave it. He never asked for their word, so they may try what they like. He forbids Aronnax to raise the subject again. Ned vows to escape whatever the weather.

On May 13 a hurricane strikes off Long Island. Instead of diving, Nemo straps himself to the platform and faces it, staring into the lightning as if courting death, and Aronnax ties himself beside him. Near midnight Nemo finally takes the ship down, and at fifty meters the sea is perfectly calm.

chapters.title: In Latitude 47° 24′ and Longitude 17° 28′
chapters.summary: Driven east by the storm, the Nautilus crosses the Grand Banks, follows the transatlantic telegraph cable, and circles off Ireland and England. Nemo pinpoints one spot, dives, and shows Aronnax the wreck of the French warship Avenger, sunk there seventy-four years ago to the day.
details: The storm ends any hope of escape near New York or the St. Lawrence, and Ned shuts himself away like Nemo. The Nautilus passes over a seafloor littered with shipwrecks, then the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, thick with cod and fishing lines. Conseil is amazed that cod aren't flat and refuses to count their eleven million eggs. Off Heart's Content the ship follows the Atlantic telegraph cable, which Conseil takes for a sea snake, and Aronnax tells the story of how it was laid.

Near Ireland, Aronnax wonders whether Nemo will land them in Britain or show him France. Instead the ship turns south past Cape Clear and Land's End, skips the English Channel, and spends two days circling, apparently hunting for an exact spot. Nemo, gloomier than ever, takes the sun's position himself. On June 1, with an unidentified steamship visible on the horizon, he finishes his sights and says only, "It's right here!"

The Nautilus sinks to the bottom beside an old, shell-crusted wreck. Nemo tells its history: a seventy-four-gun ship that fought in the American war, renamed by the French Republic in 1794. On June 1 of that year, at this exact spot, it chose to sink with its 356 men rather than surrender, its flag nailed up and its crew shouting "Long live the Republic!" Aronnax names it: the Avenger. "A splendid name," Nemo murmurs.

chapters.title: A Mass Execution
chapters.summary: An unidentified warship opens fire on the Nautilus. Nemo raises his black flag, refuses to tell Aronnax the ship's nationality, leads it on through the night, and at dawn rams it below the waterline, watching it sink with all hands before kneeling in tears before a portrait of a woman and two children.
details: As the Nautilus surfaces, a cannon sounds. A warship with no flag, an ironclad with a ram, is steaming toward them and firing. Aronnax realizes that since Ned's harpoon struck the "narwhale" from the Abraham Lincoln, the world must know it is a vessel with men inside, and that nations are hunting it. He begins to suspect that the night they were locked in the cell, and the dead man in the coral cemetery, were part of Nemo's vengeance.

Ned tries to wave a handkerchief and Nemo knocks him down. Nemo hoists his black flag, shouts at the "ship of an accursed nation," and tells Aronnax he will sink it. He will not say what country it comes from. He will not sink it beside the Avenger, either. When Aronnax tries once more to stop him, Nemo cries that he is the law and the judge. He is the oppressed, and his oppressors have destroyed everything he loved: country, wife, children, father and mother.

All night the Nautilus draws the warship on, keeping just out of range, while the three companions wait for a chance to swim to it. At dawn the crew clears the platform for action, and as the friends move to escape the hatch slams shut and the ship dives. It strikes the warship below its armor and passes through it "like a sailmaker's needle through canvas."

Aronnax rushes to the lounge and, unable to look away, watches the ship sink, its men clinging to the masts until the sea takes them. Nemo watches to the end. Then he goes into his room, and Aronnax sees him kneel and sob before a portrait of a young woman and two small children.

chapters.title: The Last Words of Captain Nemo
chapters.summary: The Nautilus flees north and wanders aimlessly for weeks with no one at the helm in sight. Ned plans an escape in the skiff; as Aronnax slips past Nemo at the organ, the captain cries "Enough!", and the skiff is torn loose just as the ship is caught in the Maelstrom.
details: Horrified, Aronnax feels Nemo has made him a witness to his revenge. The Nautilus races up through the English Channel into the northern seas and then drifts for perhaps fifteen or twenty days in Arctic fog. No positions are marked, and Nemo, his officer and the crew are never seen. Ned sinks into silence, and Conseil watches him for fear he will kill himself.

One morning Ned whispers that land is twenty miles off and nobody seems to be on watch. They will escape that night in the skiff, where he has hidden food and water. Aronnax agrees. He spends his last hour aboard among the treasures of the museum, packs his notes, and listens to Nemo pacing in his room, half wanting to face him. In his mind, Nemo swells into the Spirit of the Seas.

At ten o'clock, with mournful organ music playing, Aronnax creeps through the dark lounge. Nemo rises and drifts toward him like a ghost, sobbing, and murmurs his last words: "O almighty God! Enough! Enough!" Aronnax runs to the skiff, where Ned and Conseil are waiting.

As Ned unbolts the skiff, the crew starts shouting a single word: "Maelstrom!" The Nautilus has been caught, whether by accident or on purpose, in the great whirlpool off Norway. While the ship spins and strains, the skiff's bolts give way and it is flung into the whirlpool. Aronnax hits his head and loses consciousness.

chapters.title: Conclusion
chapters.summary: Aronnax wakes in a fisherman's hut in the Lofoten Islands with Ned and Conseil safe beside him. While he waits for a ship home, he wonders what became of the Nautilus and Captain Nemo.
details: Aronnax has no idea how the skiff escaped the Maelstrom. He comes to in a fisherman's hut on one of the Lofoten Islands, with Ned and Conseil safe at his bedside. They wait for the steamer that comes twice a month while he reviews his account, which he insists is complete and exact: 20,000 leagues in less than ten months.

He ends with questions. Did the Nautilus survive the whirlpool? Is Nemo alive and still taking revenge? Will his manuscript ever wash ashore and reveal his name? Would the sunken warship's nationality reveal his? Aronnax hopes the hate in Nemo's heart has been quieted, that the executioner is gone and the scientist lives on. He ends by saying that only two men have earned the right to answer Ecclesiastes' question about the soundless depths: Captain Nemo and himself.
